claim: 18 participants (13 female) took part in the study.
source: 18 participants (13 female) took part in the study.
evidence: Directly stated participant demographics in the manuscript.

claim: All participants were between 18 and 31 years of age with a mean of 22 years.
source: All participants were recruited from the Princeton undergraduate and graduate student population and were between 18 and 31 years of age (mean = 22 years).
evidence: Directly stated participant age range and mean in the manuscript.

claim: Duration estimates were correlated with neural pattern distance in the right entorhinal cortex.
source: Our ROI analyses found that duration estimates were correlated with the neural pattern distance between two clips at encoding in the right entorhinal cortex.
evidence: Main finding reported in the abstract with statistical support.

claim: Whole-brain searchlight analyses revealed a cluster spanning the right anterior temporal lobe.
source: Moreover, whole-brain searchlight analyses revealed a cluster spanning the right anterior temporal lobe.
evidence: Main finding reported in the abstract with statistical support.

claim: Retrospective time judgments are driven by 'drift' in contextual representations.
source: Our findings provide convergent support for the hypothesis that retrospective time judgments are driven by 'drift' in contextual representations supported by these regions.
evidence: Interpretation of findings stated in the abstract.

claim: The 6-min intervals were judged to be significantly longer than the 2-min intervals.
source: On average, across participants, the 6-min intervals (M=5.70 min, SD=3.06) were judged to be significantly longer than the 2-min intervals (M=3.69 min, SD=1.96), t(17) = 5.20, p<10-4 (see Figure 2A).
evidence: Statistical test result with specific values and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Participants were better at distinguishing 6-min intervals from 2-min intervals when they were confident.
source: The difference score was significantly higher for high-confidence intervals (M=2.43, SD=1.82) than for all intervals (M=2.01, SD=1.64), t(17)=2.33, p=0.0324.
evidence: Statistical comparison showing confidence effect on accuracy.

claim: The average correlation between two random groups of participants was 0.64 (SD=0.09) for 2-min intervals.
source: The average correlation between the two groups was 0.64 (SD=0.09) for 2-min intervals and 0.54 (SD=0.15) for 6-min intervals (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Reliability analysis result with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Naïve participants estimated 6-min intervals to be longer than 2-min intervals.
source: We found that naïve participants estimated 6-min intervals (M=6.21 min, SD=1.91) to be longer than 2-min intervals (M=5.63 min, SD=1.74; t(16)=2.62, p=0.019), suggesting that the similarity between two clips carried some information about the temporal distance between them.
evidence: Statistical test result from control experiment.

claim: Original participants were significantly more accurate at distinguishing 6-min intervals from 2-min intervals than naïve participants.
source: The difference score was significantly higher for our original participants (M=2.01 min, SD=1.64 min) than for naïve participants (M=0.59 min, SD=0.91 min), t(26.86)=−3.22, p<0.005.
evidence: Statistical comparison between original and naïve participants.

claim: The number of event boundaries in an interval was significantly correlated with duration estimates from the original experiment (r = 0.49, 95% CI [0.27, 0.57]).
source: We found that the mean number of boundaries in an interval was significantly correlated with the mean duration estimates from our original experiment (r = 0.49, 95% CI [0.27, 0.57]; Figure 3).
evidence: Correlation analysis with confidence intervals and figure reference.

claim: The number of event boundaries did not significantly correlate with duration estimates of naïve participants (r=0.09, 95% CI [−0.05, 0.21]).
source: Importantly, we found that the number of event boundaries in an interval did not significantly correlate with duration estimates of naïve participants (r=0.09, 95% CI [−0.05, 0.21]; Figure 3).
evidence: Correlation analysis with confidence intervals and figure reference.

claim: The right entorhinal cortex and right pars orbitalis showed a significant positive correlation between pattern change and duration estimates (q<0.05).
source: Out of the regions selected a priori, the right entorhinal cortex and right pars orbitalis showed a significant positive correlation between pattern change and duration estimates for high-confidence 2-minute intervals (q<0.05).
evidence: ROI analysis result with FDR correction.

claim: The left caudal anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) showed significant positive correlations between pattern change and duration estimates (q<0.1).
source: Out of the 84 regions tested (42 in each hemisphere), the right entorhinal cortex, right pars orbitalis, and left caudal anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) showed significant positive correlations between pattern change and duration estimates (q<0.1).
evidence: Whole-brain ROI analysis result with FDR correction.

claim: The right entorhinal cortex, right amygdala, and right insula showed a significant positive correlation between pattern change and duration estimates in the within-interval analysis (q<0.05).
source: Out of the regions selected a priori, the right entorhinal cortex, right amygdala, and right insula showed a significant positive correlation between pattern change and duration estimates for high-confidence 2-minute intervals (q<0.05).
evidence: Within-interval ROI analysis result with FDR correction.

claim: The right entorhinal cortex is the only region with significant effects in both the within-interval analysis (Cohen's d = 0.83) and the within-participant analysis (Cohen's d = 0.79).
source: Importantly, the right entorhinal cortex is the only region with significant effects in both the within-interval analysis (Cohen's d = 0.83) and the within-participant analysis (Cohen's d = 0.79).
evidence: Comparison of effect sizes across two analysis types.

claim: The within-participant searchlight analysis found a significant cluster in the right anterior temporal lobe (p=0.034, FWE-corrected).
source: When excluding low-confidence intervals, we found a significant cluster in the right anterior temporal lobe (p=0.034, FWE-corrected; Center of Gravity MNI coordinates (x, y, z) in mm: [45.6, −5.53, −21.7]; cluster size=572 voxels in 3 mm MNI space).
evidence: Searchlight analysis result with FWE correction and coordinates.

claim: The within-interval searchlight analysis found a significant cluster in the right anterior temporal lobe (p=0.019, FWE-corrected).
source: Similarly to the within-participant searchlight, we found a significant cluster in the right anterior temporal lobe (p=0.019, FWE-corrected; Center of Gravity MNI coordinates (x, y, z) in mm: [32.1, −10.2, −18.7]; cluster size=535 voxels in 3 mm MNI space).
evidence: Searchlight analysis result with FWE correction and coordinates.

claim: The right entorhinal cortex had the slowest pattern change in the brain, ranking 3rd, 4th and 1st across three procedures.
source: Moreover, the mean FWHM in the right entorhinal cortex was one of the largest among all 84 regions, ranking 3rd, 4th and 1st in the brain across the three procedures.
evidence: Analysis of pattern change speed across brain regions.

claim: Duration estimates systematically decreased as a function of position in the story.
source: We found that duration estimates systematically decreased as a function of position in the story, with earlier intervals being estimated as longer than later intervals (Figure 11).
evidence: Observation of temporal trend in duration estimates with figure reference.

claim: The correlation between the estimated duration of an interval and its time in the story was consistently negative across participants (M=−0.40, SD= 0.22; t(16)=−7.59, p<0.00001).
source: The correlation between the estimated duration of an interval and its time in the story was consistently negative across participants (M=−0.40, SD= 0.22; t(16)=−7.59, p<0.00001).
evidence: Statistical test of correlation between duration estimates and story position.

claim: The mean correlation between the actual and estimated temporal position on the timeline of the story was r=0.885 (SD=0.05).
source: The mean correlation (across participants) between the actual and estimated temporal position on the timeline of the story was r=0.885 (SD=0.05), suggesting that participants remembered the temporal position of each clip extremely well (p<10–21).
evidence: Statistical measure of temporal memory accuracy.

claim: Accuracy of timeline placements was significantly correlated with encoding activity in large clusters of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and medial prefrontal cortex (p=0.008, FWE-corrected).
source: We found that the accuracy (negative error) of timeline placements was significantly correlated with encoding activity in large clusters of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and medial prefrontal cortex, including dorsomedial PFC and anterior cingulate (p=0.008, FWE-corrected; Center of Gravity MNI coordinates (x, y, z) in mm: [−20, 34.8, 28.4]; cluster size = 1121 voxels in 3 mm MNI space), as well as sub-threshold clusters in the medial parietal cortex, including precuneus and posterior cingulate (p=0.058, FWE-corrected; Center of Gravity MNI coordinates (x, y, z) in mm: [−10.5, −54, 16.1]; cluster size = 419 voxels), and left superior temporal gyrus (p=0.098, FWE-corrected; Center of Gravity MNI coordinates (x, y, z) in mm: [−56.9, −19.1, −3.72]; cluster size = 270 voxels).
evidence: Replication analysis result with statistical correction and coordinates.

claim: Mental context refers to aspects of our mental state that tend to persist over a relatively long time scale.
source: According to extant theories of context and memory (see Manning et al., 2014, for a review), mental context refers to aspects of our mental state that tend to persist over a relatively long time scale; this encompasses our representation of slowly-changing aspects of the external world (e.g., what room we are in) as well as other slowly-changing aspects of our internal mental state (e.g., our current plans).
evidence: Definition cited from existing literature.

claim: Slowly-changing contextual features can be episodically associated with more quickly-changing aspects of the world.
source: Crucially, these theories posit that slowly-changing contextual features can be episodically associated with more quickly-changing aspects of the world (e.g., stimuli that appear at a particular moment in time; Mensink and Raaijmakers, 1988; Howard and Kahana, 2002).
evidence: Theoretical claim supported by citations.

claim: Bower (1972) first proposed that we could determine how long ago an item occurred by comparing our current context with the context associated with the remembered item.
source: Bower (1972) first proposed that we could determine how long ago an item occurred by comparing our current context with the context associated with the remembered item.
evidence: Historical attribution of theoretical proposal.

claim: The degree of context change is a better predictor of duration judgments than alternative explanations, such as the number of items remembered from the interval.
source: In parallel, researchers in the domain of retrospective time estimation have shown that the degree of context change is a better predictor of duration judgments than alternative explanations, such as the number of items remembered from the interval (Block and Reed, 1978; Block, 1990, 1992).
evidence: Summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: Changes in task processing, environmental context, emotions, and event boundaries lead to overestimation of past durations.
source: Indeed, changes in task processing (Block and Reed, 1978; Sahakyan and Smith, 2014), environmental context (Block, 1982), and emotions (Pollatos et al., 2014), as well as event boundaries (Poynter, 1983; Zakay et al., 1994; Faber and Gennari, 2015), lead to overestimation of past durations.
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: The medial temporal lobe (MTL) and lateral prefrontal cortex (PFC) are implicated in representing contextual information.
source: Extensive prior work has implicated the medial temporal lobe (MTL) and lateral prefrontal cortex (PFC) in representing contextual information (Polyn and Kahana, 2008; for reviews of MTL contributions to representing context, see Eichenbaum et al., 2007, and Ritchey and Ranganath, 2012; for related computational modeling work, see Howard and Eichenbaum, 2013).
evidence: Summary of prior work with multiple citations.

claim: Greater change in hippocampal activity patterns between two stimuli predicted better memory for the order in which the stimuli occurred in rats.
source: Manns et al. (2007) recorded from rat hippocampus during an odor memory task; they found that greater change in hippocampal activity patterns between two stimuli predicted better memory for the order in which the stimuli occurred.
evidence: Summary of findings from cited animal study.

claim: The degree to which activity patterns in rostrolateral prefrontal cortex changed during encoding predicted better memory for the temporal position of a stimulus.
source: In the human neuroimaging literature, Jenkins and Ranganath (2010) found that the degree to which activity patterns in rostrolateral prefrontal cortex changed during the encoding of a stimulus predicted better memory for the temporal position of that stimulus in the experiment.
evidence: Summary of findings from cited human neuroimaging study.

claim: Greater pattern distance between two stimuli at encoding in the hippocampus, medial and anterior prefrontal cortex predicted better order memory.
source: Jenkins and Ranganath (2016) also showed that greater pattern distance between two stimuli at encoding in the hippocampus, medial and anterior prefrontal cortex predicted better order memory.
evidence: Summary of findings from cited study.

claim: Patterns of fMRI activity in left hippocampus were more similar for pairs of stimuli that were later estimated to have occurred closer together in time.
source: Ezzyat and Davachi (2014) found that patterns of fMRI activity in left hippocampus were more similar for pairs of stimuli that were later estimated to have occurred closer together in time, despite equivalent time passage between all pairs (a little less than a minute).
evidence: Summary of findings from cited study.

claim: Estimating time prospectively engages different mechanisms than retrospective estimation.
source: Knowing that they would have to estimate durations between stimuli could have changed participants' strategy and enhanced their attention to time (for evidence that estimating time prospectively engages different mechanisms, see Hicks et al., 1976, and Zakay and Block, 2004).
evidence: Theoretical claim supported by citations.

claim: Lesions of the lateral entorhinal cortex in rodents impair discrimination between novel and familiar associations of object and place, object and non-spatial context, or place and context.
source: Lesions of the lateral entorhinal cortex in rodents have shown that this region is necessary for discriminating between novel and familiar associations of object and place, object and non-spatial context, or place and context, while leaving non-associative forms of memory unaffected (Buckmaster et al., 2004; Wilson et al., 2013a; 2013b).
evidence: Summary of findings from cited animal lesion studies.

claim: Neurons in the medial entorhinal cortex exhibited greater context sensitivity and greater modulation by task-relevant mnemonic information than hippocampal neurons.
source: Moreover, electrophysiological recordings in rats performing a spatial memory task showed that neurons in the medial entorhinal cortex exhibited greater context sensitivity and greater modulation by task-relevant mnemonic information than hippocampal neurons, while hippocampal neurons carried more specific spatial information (Lipton et al., 2007).
evidence: Summary of findings from cited electrophysiology study.

claim: Medial entorhinal neurons exhibited longer firing periods, which could bind a series of hippocampal representations of distinct events.
source: Medial entorhinal neurons also exhibited longer firing periods, which led the authors to propose that they could bind a series of hippocampal representations of distinct events (Lipton and Eichenbaum, 2008).
evidence: Summary of findings and interpretation from cited study.

claim: Noulhiane et al. (2007) found that the degree of left entorhinal, left perirhinal and left temporopolar cortex damage correlated with the degree to which patients overestimated minutes-long intervals in retrospect.
source: Noulhiane et al. (2007) used a retrospective behavioral paradigm similar to ours in patients with unilateral MTL lesions. In that study, participants were asked to estimate the temporal distance between object pictures that had been randomly inserted into a silent documentary film. They found that the degree of left entorhinal, left perirhinal and left temporopolar cortex damage correlated with the degree to which patients overestimated minutes-long intervals in retrospect.
evidence: Summary of findings from cited patient study.

claim: Bilateral inactivation of the hippocampus impaired rats' ability to discriminate between similarly long durations, such as 8 and 12 minutes, but not between less similar intervals, such as 3 and 12 minutes.
source: For related evidence from the animal literature, see Jacobs et al., 2013, who showed that bilateral inactivation of the hippocampus impaired rats' ability to discriminate between similarly long durations, such as 8 and 12 minutes, but not between less similar intervals, such as 3 and 12 minutes.
evidence: Summary of findings from cited animal study.

claim: Caudal ACC activity increases in response to shifts in task contingencies.
source: Caudal ACC activity has been shown to increase in response to shifts in task contingencies (see Shenhav et al., 2013, for a review) and there is converging evidence that ACC responses are important for adjusting behavior to unexpected changes by increasing attention and learning rate (Bryden et al., 2011; Behrens et al., 2007; McGuire et al., 2014).
evidence: Summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: The ACC only responds to surprising outcomes when they necessitate updating beliefs about the current state of the world.
source: O'Reilly et al. (2013) have provided evidence that the ACC only responds to surprising outcomes when they necessitate updating beliefs about the current state of the world.
evidence: Summary of findings from cited study.

claim: The middle temporal gyrus and temporal pole are involved in narrative comprehension.
source: Prior work has suggested that the middle temporal gyrus and temporal pole are involved in narrative comprehension (Ferstl et al., 2008; Mar, 2004) and narrative item memory (Hasson et al., 2007; Maguire et al., 1999).
evidence: Summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: Activity within the right perirhinal cortex to the right middle temporal gyrus gradually increases within events and this increase predicts the degree to which memories become clustered within events.
source: Ezzyat and Davachi (2011) found a similarly located cluster (extending from the right perirhinal cortex to the right middle temporal gyrus) to be involved in integrating information within narrative events. In particular, they showed that activity within these regions gradually increases within events and that this increase predicts the degree to which memories become clustered within events.
evidence: Summary of findings from cited study.

claim: Retrospective time judgments increase with the number of events an interval contains.
source: Retrospective time judgments have been shown to increase with the number of events an interval contains (Poynter, 1983; Zakay et al., 1994; Faber and Gennari, 2015), suggesting that brain regions involved in clustering memories by events may carry important information for estimating durations.
evidence: Summary of findings from cited literature with inference.

claim: Brain regions at the top of the processing hierarchy integrate information over longer time scales.
source: This is in line with findings that brain regions at the top of the processing hierarchy (furthest from the primary perceptual areas) integrate information over longer time scales and are therefore best suited for representing abstract information extracted from multiple streams of sensory observations (Stephens et al., 2013; Lerner et al., 2011).
evidence: Summary of findings from cited literature.

claim: The medial prefrontal and medial parietal cortex may be important for maintaining narrative information over minutes-long timescales.
source: These regions may be important for maintaining narrative information over minutes-long timescales (Lerner et al., 2011; Hasson et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2015), which might explain why their activity predicted temporal context memory for clips from an auditory story, but did not appear in Jenkins and Ranganath (2010), where participants recalled the timing of trials which were not linked by a narrative.
evidence: Inference based on cited literature.

claim: The clusters found overlap highly with the 'posterior medial network', which has been consistently implicated in episodic memory, episodic simulation and theory of mind.
source: Moreover, our clusters overlap highly with the 'posterior medial network' (Ritchey and Ranganath, 2012), which has been consistently implicated in episodic memory, episodic simulation and theory of mind.
evidence: Comparison with cited literature.

claim: Participants were compensated $20/hr for the scanning session, and $12/hr for the behavioral session.
source: Participants were compensated $20/hr for the scanning session, and $12/hr for the behavioral session.
evidence: Directly stated compensation information.

claim: The story used was a radio adaptation of 'Tunnel Under the World' written by Frederik Pohl, originally aired on 'X Minus One' in 1956.
source: While in the scanner, participants listened to a 25-minute-long radio adaptation of a science fiction story called 'Tunnel Under the World' (written by Frederik Pohl), originally aired on the radio drama series, 'X Minus One', in 1956.
evidence: Directly stated stimulus information.

claim: 24 of the clip pairs were 2 minutes apart and 19 of the pairs were 6 minutes apart.
source: To control for the objective passage of time, we ensured that 24 of the clip pairs were 2 minutes apart and 19 of the pairs were 6 minutes apart.
evidence: Directly stated experimental design detail.

claim: Participants were unaware that clip pairs had fixed interval durations of 2 or 6 minutes.
source: Debriefing showed that participants were unaware of this manipulation, and the high variability of duration estimates for both the 2 and 6-min intervals further confirmed that they were unaware of the fixed interval durations.
evidence: Debriefing data and behavioral variability.

claim: Functional images were acquired using a T2*-weighted echo planer imaging (EPI) pulse sequence with TR of 1500 ms, TE of 28 ms, and flip angle of 64°.
source: Functional images were acquired using a T2*-weighted echo planer imaging (EPI) pulse sequence (repetition time [TR], 1500 ms; echo time [TE], 28 ms; flip angle, 64°), each volume comprising 27 slices of 4 mm thickness.
evidence: Directly stated MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: A high-pass filter cut-off of 480 s was selected for the analysis.
source: Out of the filters tested (240 s – 720 s), a cut-off of 480 s was selected to be the gentlest (i.e. the longest) filter that reduced the magnitude of inter-subject correlations in ventricles and CSF, such that they were significantly below the correlations in most grey matter regions.
evidence: Methodological decision based on data quality analysis.

claim: Six-minute intervals were excluded from the fMRI analysis because neural pattern change at this timescale could not be successfully dissociated from low-frequency scanner noise.
source: Six-minute intervals were excluded from the fMRI analysis, since we could not successfully dissociate neural pattern change at this timescale from low-frequency scanner noise (see Methodological challenges with analyzing pattern distance over long time scales in the Materials and methods).
evidence: Methodological limitation explained in the text.

claim: Having memory of the story induced a qualitatively different pattern of behavior and produced significantly more accurate duration estimates.
source: In other words, there is a reliable component of our original participants' behavior that cannot be captured by accounting for the perceptual and semantic similarity between clips. In summary, having memory of the story induced a qualitatively different pattern of behavior and produced significantly more accurate duration estimates.
evidence: Inference from statistical comparisons.

claim: The number of event boundaries carries information about temporal context that is not contained within the clips alone.
source: This suggests that the number of event boundaries carries information about temporal context that is not contained within the clips alone, and that our original participants' estimates were influenced by their memory of this contextual information.
evidence: Inference from comparison of original and naïve participants.

claim: The effect sizes are similar between within-participant and within-interval analyses for the right entorhinal cortex, showing that perceptual or semantic differences in content between clips are not the main factor driving the correlation.
source: If neural pattern distance between two clips in entorhinal cortex were driven solely by changes in clip content, we would have expected the correlation with duration estimates to be larger for the within-participant analysis (where story content differed across intervals) than for the within-interval analysis (where story content is held constant). The fact that the effect sizes are similar shows that perceptual or semantic differences in content between the two clips are not the main factor driving the correlation between duration estimates and neural pattern change in this region.
evidence: Inference from comparison of effect sizes across analyses.

claim: The fixed effect of naïve estimates was positive in all models and its confidence intervals did not include zero in 80% of the models.
source: The fixed effect of naïve estimates was positive in all models and its confidence intervals did not include zero in 80% of the models.
evidence: Result from mixed-effects modeling.

claim: The fixed effect of neural pattern distance in left caudal ACC and right entorhinal cortex exhibited confidence intervals that did not include zero in the mixed-effects model.
source: However, even under this control, the fixed effect of neural pattern distance in left caudal ACC and right entorhinal cortex exhibited confidence intervals that did not include zero (Figure 7).
evidence: Result from mixed-effects modeling with figure reference.

claim: Including naïve duration estimates as a covariate did not significantly weaken the relationship between neural pattern distance and duration estimates in the right entorhinal cortex and left caudal ACC.
source: Importantly, including the naïve duration estimates as a covariate in the model did not significantly weaken the relationship between neural pattern distance and duration estimates in these regions (though the effects were slightly lower numerically).
evidence: Comparison of model results with and without covariate.

claim: The FWHMs in the right entorhinal cortex were consistently larger across participants than the FWHMs in the right transverse temporal cortex, right banks of the superior temporal sulcus, and right superior temporal cortex across all three procedures.
source: Across all three procedures, a right-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test indicated that the FWHMs in the right entorhinal cortex were consistently larger across participants than the FWHMs in the right transverse temporal cortex (p<0.00005, p<0.0005 and p<0.00005), the right banks of the superior temporal sulcus (p<0.001, p<0.001 and p<0.0005) and the right superior temporal cortex (p<0.005, p=0.06 and p<0.0005).
evidence: Statistical comparison of pattern change speed across regions.

claim: Single voxels and multivariate patterns in entorhinal cortex changed consistently more slowly than those in regions involved in auditory and language processing.
source: Thus, single voxels and multivariate patterns in entorhinal cortex changed consistently more slowly than those in regions involved in auditory and language processing.
evidence: Summary of statistical comparisons.

claim: The left caudal ACC ranked 66th, 67th and 46th out of 84 regions across the three procedures for speed of pattern change.
source: On the other hand, the left caudal ACC ranked 66th, 67th and 46th out of 84 regions across the three procedures, suggesting that it did not exhibit slow signal change relative to the rest of the brain.
evidence: Ranking analysis of pattern change speed.

claim: Patterns in the left caudal ACC changed only slightly more slowly than those in primary auditory cortex.
source: Thus, patterns in the left caudal ACC changed only slightly more slowly than those in primary auditory cortex.
evidence: Summary of statistical comparisons.

claim: The right entorhinal cortex, along with other regions of the anterior and medial temporal lobe, orbitofrontal cortex and frontal pole, had the slowest pattern change in the brain.
source: Taken together, all three variants of the analysis showed that the right entorhinal cortex, along with other regions of the anterior and medial temporal lobe, orbitofrontal cortex and frontal pole, had the slowest pattern change in the brain.
evidence: Summary of pattern change speed analysis.

claim: There was no consistent correlation between pattern change during an interval and its time in the story for the right entorhinal cortex, right pars orbitalis, left caudal ACC, right amygdala, or right insula.
source: However, there was no consistent correlation between pattern change during an interval and its time in the story for the right entorhinal cortex (M=0.03, SD=0.21; t(16)= 0.65; p=0.53), the right pars orbitalis (M=−0.10, SD=0.22; t(16)=−1.83, p=0.09), the left caudal ACC (M=−0.05, SD=0.18; t(16)=−1.15, p=0.27), the right amygdala (M=−0.02, SD=0.23; t(16)=−0.28, p=0.78) or the right insula (M=−0.08, SD=0.25; t(16)=−1.34, p=0.20).
evidence: Statistical tests showing no correlation with story position.

claim: The relationship between duration estimates and pattern dissimilarity in these regions was not driven by a shared effect of story position.
source: These results suggest that the relationship between duration estimates and pattern dissimilarity in these regions was not driven by a shared effect of story position.
evidence: Inference from lack of correlation with story position.

claim: Pattern dissimilarity in these regions correlated with more fine-grained variations in the estimated durations of nearby intervals.
source: Rather, it seems that pattern dissimilarity in these regions correlated with more fine-grained variations in the estimated durations of nearby intervals (Figure 11).
evidence: Inference from analysis with figure reference.

claim: Almost all brain patterns changed more at the end of the story than at the beginning when analyzing unfiltered data.
source: When we did this, we found that neural pattern change in the unfiltered data showed a consistent correlation in the opposite direction: almost all brain patterns changed more at the end of the story than at the beginning, including the CSF and white matter (q<0.05, FDR), suggesting that a signal unrelated to neural processing, such as scanner drift or motion, may cause activity patterns to change more as time passes (see Figure 11—source data 1).
evidence: Analysis of unfiltered data showing artifact.

claim: The within-interval searchlight cluster was located more medially than the within-participant searchlight cluster.
source: The within-interval searchlight cluster was located more medially than the within-participant searchlight cluster, though the two overlapped in the right amygdala, right temporal pole, and the cerebral white matter of the right anterior temporal lobe.
evidence: Spatial comparison of searchlight results.

claim: The within-interval searchlight cluster overlapped with the right entorhinal cortex ROI.
source: Moreover, the within-interval searchlight cluster overlapped with the right entorhinal cortex ROI (see green voxels, Figure 10).
evidence: Spatial overlap observation with figure reference.

claim: The difference in regions that passed significance threshold between ROI and searchlight analyses is likely due to the difference in shapes between the searchlight cube and the anatomical masks.
source: The difference in the set of regions that passed the significance threshold between the ROI and searchlight analyses is very likely due to the difference in shapes between the searchlight cube and the anatomical masks.
evidence: Methodological explanation for differences in results.

claim: Following anatomy is particularly important for small, elongated regions like entorhinal cortex and caudal ACC, which are unlikely to be perfectly aligned across participants.
source: Following the anatomy is particularly important for small, elongated regions like entorhinal cortex and caudal ACC, which are unlikely to be perfectly aligned across participants.
evidence: Methodological consideration based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: Anatomical ROI analyses were performed entirely in native space, making them more suitable for idiosyncratically shaped regions.
source: On the other hand, anatomical ROI analyses were performed entirely in native space, making them more suitable for idiosyncratically shaped regions.
evidence: Methodological explanation.

claim: The findings are consistent with those of Stephens et al. (2013), who showed that auditory cortex regions processing momentary stimulus features had intrinsically faster dynamics than higher-order regions that integrated information over longer time scales.
source: Our findings are consistent with those of Stephens et al. (2013), who showed that auditory cortex regions processing momentary stimulus features had intrinsically faster dynamics than higher-order regions that integrated information over longer time scales (see also Lerner et al., 2011).
evidence: Comparison with cited literature.

claim: The decrease in mean duration estimates with story position may be due to the relationship between the number of event boundaries and duration estimates.
source: In our story, there was a strong negative correlation between the mean number of event boundaries per interval and the position of the interval in the story (r=−0.77). Thus, the decrease in mean duration estimates with story position may be due to the relationship between the number of event boundaries and duration estimates (see Behavioral results).
evidence: Inference from correlation analysis.

claim: The result showing decreased duration estimates over time may be a replication of the positive time-order effect.
source: This result may be a replication of the positive time-order effect: the finding that people judge earlier durations in a series of durations to be longer than later durations (Block, 1982, 1985; Brown and Stubbs, 1988).
evidence: Interpretation with citations to related literature.

claim: The positive time-order effect has been interpreted to mean that context usually changes more rapidly at the start of a novel episode.
source: The effect has been interpreted to mean that context usually changes more rapidly at the start of a novel episode (Block, 1982, 1986).
evidence: Interpretation from cited literature.

claim: Participants were scanned in a 3T full-body Skyra MRI scanner (Siemens, Munich, Germany) with a 20-channel head coil.
source: Participants were scanned in a 3T full-body Skyra MRI scanner (Siemens, Munich, Germany) with a 20-channel head coil.
evidence: Directly stated MRI equipment information.

claim: Anatomical images were acquired using a T1-weighted MPRAGE pulse sequence with TR of 2300 ms, TE of 3.08 ms, flip angle 9°, and 0.89 mm³ resolution.
source: Anatomical images were acquired using a T1-weighted magnetization-prepared rapid-acquisition gradient echo (MPRAGE) pulse sequence (TR, 2300 ms; TE, 3.08 ms; flip angle 9°; 0.89 mm3 resolution; FOV, 256 mm2).
evidence: Directly stated MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Participants were provided with MRI compatible in-ear mono earbuds (Model S14, Sensimetrics Corporation, Malden, MA).
source: Participants were provided with MRI compatible in-ear mono earbuds (Model S14, Sensimetrics Corporation, Malden, MA), which provided the same audio input to each ear.
evidence: Directly stated equipment information.

claim: The sample size was chosen to be in the same range as previous fMRI studies that had used naturalistic stimuli to study memory.
source: Therefore, rather than performing a power analysis, we chose a sample size that was in the same range as previous fMRI studies that had used naturalistic stimuli to study memory (Lerner et al., 2011, n=11 per condition; Chen et al., 2015, n=13, 14 and 24 per condition; Chen et al., 2016, n=22 [5 excluded]), as well as fMRI studies that had related neural pattern distance to mnemonic judgments (Ezzyat and Davachi, 2011, n=19; Jenkins and Ranganath, 2010, n=16 (1 excluded); Ezzyat and Davachi, 2014, n=21 (3 excluded), Jenkins and Ranganath, 2016, n=17).
evidence: Justification for sample size based on prior literature.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained for all participants in accordance with the Princeton Institutional Review Board regulations.
source: Written informed consent was obtained for all participants in accordance with the Princeton Institutional Review Board regulations.
evidence: Directly stated ethical compliance information.

claim: All participants were screened to ensure no neurological or psychiatric disorders.
source: All participants were screened to ensure no neurological or psychiatric disorders.
evidence: Directly stated participant screening criteria.

claim: Participants had complete control over the pacing of the time perception test.
source: Participants had complete control over the pacing of the test. On each question, they initiated the playing of the clips, and were able to replay the clips if they missed them the first time.
evidence: Directly stated experimental procedure detail.

claim: Clip pairs were identical across participants, but the order in which the pairs were presented was randomized.
source: Clip pairs were identical across participants, but the order in which the pairs were presented was randomized.
evidence: Directly stated experimental design detail.

claim: A separate group of 9 participants listened to the story and pressed a button every time they felt an event boundary was occurring.
source: A separate group of participants (n=9) listened to the story and was asked to press a button every time they felt an event boundary was occurring.
evidence: Directly stated experimental procedure for event boundary test.

claim: 17 participants who had never heard the story were given an identical time perception test.
source: To ensure that participants were using their memory of the story to judge temporal distance, we ran a control experiment in which 17 participants who had never heard the story were given the exact same memory test.
evidence: Directly stated control experiment design.

claim: During debriefing, naïve participants reported making duration estimates based on the perceptual and semantic similarity between the two clips.
source: During debriefing, participants reported making duration estimates based on the perceptual and semantic similarity between the two clips (e.g., which character voices were present, which background music was playing, the topic of conversation).
evidence: Debriefing data from naïve participants.

claim: The first participant completed a version of the time perception test with different specific intervals in the story.
source: Please note: the first of our 18 participants completed a version of the time perception test that differed only in the following way: the specific intervals in the story whose duration was asked about were different.
evidence: Directly stated methodological note.

claim: Segmentation was performed using FreeSurfer image analysis suite version 5.1.
source: Segmentation was performed in a semi-automated fashion using the FreeSurfer image analysis suite, which is documented and available online (version 5.1; http://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu) with details described previously (e.g. Fischl et al., 2004; Poppenk and Norman, 2014).
evidence: Directly stated software and version used.

claim: MTL regions were defined probabilistically in MNI space based on a database of manual MTL segmentations from 24 participants.
source: MTL regions, including perirhinal cortex, entorhinal cortex and parahippocampal cortex were defined probabilistically in MNI space, based on a database of manual MTL segmentations from a separate set of 24 participants.
evidence: Directly stated segmentation procedure.

claim: Voxels with a probability greater than 0.3 of being in a region were assigned to that ROI.
source: After registration, voxels with a probability greater than 0.3 of being in a region were assigned to that ROI.
evidence: Directly stated threshold for ROI assignment.

claim: The residualization procedure was always applied after removal of low-frequency components using the high-pass filter.
source: Note that this procedure was always applied after removal of low-frequency components using the high-pass filter (see below).
evidence: Directly stated order of preprocessing steps.

claim: The functional scan length was 1560 s (26 min).
source: Since the functional scan length was 1560 s (26 min), high-pass filter cut-off periods of 140 s, 240 s, 300 s, 400 s, 480 s, 600 s and 720 s were attempted.
evidence: Directly stated scan duration.

claim: Activity patterns were averaged over 5 consecutive TRs for every clip, with the 5-TR window centered on the middle of each clip.
source: Since the auditory clips were between 5 s and 10 s in duration (corresponding to about 5 volumes), we averaged the patterns over 5 consecutive TRs for every clip, with the 5-TR window centered on the middle of each clip.
evidence: Directly stated analysis procedure.

claim: Pattern dissimilarity was calculated as 1 minus the Pearson correlation between two averaged activity patterns.
source: Specifically, we calculated the dissimilarity (1 – Pearson correlation) between the two averaged activity patterns.
evidence: Directly stated distance metric.

claim: All Pearson correlation coefficients were Fisher-transformed prior to statistical testing.
source: All Pearson correlation coefficients were Fisher-transformed prior to statistical testing (Fisher, 1915).
evidence: Directly stated statistical procedure with citation.

claim: 10,000 null correlations were obtained for each ROI in every participant using phase randomization.
source: Thus, we generated a distribution of 10,000 null correlations for every ROI in every participant (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Directly stated permutation procedure with figure reference.

claim: The confidence threshold for each participant removed at least 33% of the intervals with the lowest confidence, while preserving at least 33% of the intervals with the highest confidence.
source: Since participants calibrated their confidence ratings differently (some were more prone to rate their confidence as 4/5, while others were more prone to rate it as 2/5), we picked the confidence threshold for each participant that removed at least 33% of the intervals with the lowest confidence, while preserving at least 33% of the intervals with the highest confidence.
evidence: Directly stated data filtering procedure.

claim: Family-wise error rate was controlled using FSL's randomise function (version 5.0.4).
source: Family-wise error rate was controlled using FSL's randomise function (version 5.0.4, Winkler et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly stated statistical software and version with citation.

claim: A corrected p-value was assigned to each cluster by assessing its cluster mass with respect to the null distribution of the maximum cluster mass during 10,000 permutation simulations.
source: Specifically, a corrected p-value was assigned to each cluster by assessing its cluster mass with respect to the null distribution of the maximum cluster mass during 10,000 permutation simulations (Hayasaka and Nichols, 2003; Nichols and Holmes, 2002).
evidence: Directly stated statistical procedure with citations.

claim: The within-participant searchlight analysis used cubic searchlights with 3x3x3 (27) voxels (972 mm³).
source: We ran a cubic searchlight with 3x3x3 (27) voxels (972 mm3) through the entire brain and tested for a correlation between pattern change and duration estimates in each searchlight.
evidence: Directly stated searchlight parameters.

claim: The within-interval searchlight analysis used cubic searchlights of radius 2 with 5x5x5 (125) voxels.
source: Since this transformation approximately doubles the number of brain voxels, we ran cubic searchlights of radius 2 with 5x5x5 (125) voxels through the entire brain.
evidence: Directly stated searchlight parameters.

claim: Neural pattern distance was not calculated for searchlights on the very edge of the brain with fewer than 25 voxels.
source: Neural pattern distance was not calculated for searchlights on the very edge of the brain with fewer than 25 voxels, in order to reduce noise from overly small patterns.
evidence: Directly stated data exclusion criterion.

claim: A searchlight location was excluded if fewer than 5 participants had brain voxels in that location.
source: We also excluded a searchlight location if fewer than 5 participants had brain voxels in that location.
evidence: Directly stated data exclusion criterion.

claim: The BOLD time course of every voxel was smoothed using a moving average filter of 5 TRs.
source: (As for our main analysis, the BOLD time course of every voxel was smoothed using a moving average filter of 5 TRs. This temporal smoothing was used as a de-noising technique and did not affect the results.)
evidence: Directly stated preprocessing procedure.

claim: The Full-Width Half-Maximum (FWHM) of the auto-correlation curve was defined as the number of time points (TRs) for which the auto-correlation was equal to or greater than half its maximum value.
source: To quantify this, we defined the Full-Width Half-Maximum (FWHM) of the auto-correlation curve as the number of time points (TRs) for which the auto-correlation was equal to or greater than half its maximum value (the maximum was always 1.)
evidence: Directly stated metric definition.

claim: A weak Wishart prior was imposed on the group covariances to regularize the mixed-effects model away from singularity.
source: Since such rich models often fail to converge or approach singularity given typical psychological datasets (Bates et al., 2015a), we imposed a weak Wishart prior on the group covariances, which regularizes the model away from singularity (Chung et al., 2015).
evidence: Directly stated statistical modeling procedure with citations.

claim: The duration estimates were power-transformed using the Box-Cox power transformation to mitigate heteroskedastic residuals.
source: Finally, the duration estimates are bounded at zero and positively skewed, which resulted in heteroskedastic residuals. To mitigate this, we power-transformed the duration estimates using the Box-Cox power transformation (Box and Cox, 1964).
evidence: Directly stated data transformation procedure with citation.

claim: 95% confidence intervals of the fixed-effects parameter estimates were computed using the asymptotic Gaussian approximation.
source: We computed 0.95 confidence intervals of β using the asymptotic Gaussian approximation (called the 'Wald approximation' in lme4) based on the estimated local curvature of the likelihood surface.
evidence: Directly stated statistical procedure.
